name: Calabresella
description: Calabresella (also known as Terziglio) is an Italian three-player point-trick game with bidding. It is closely related to Tressette. The main aim is to capture aces and take the last trick, which is difficult because there are no trumps. The game features an unusual card order with threes as the highest cards.

history.origins:
Country/Region of Origin: Italy
Time Period: Traditional game, documented since 19th century
Historical Development: Related to Tressette and other Italian point-trick games. An American variation was described in 1870 by Cavendish (Henry Jones). The name Calabresella suggests origins in Calabria region.
Cultural Significance: Played throughout Italy, particularly popular in traditional card-playing circles.
timeline: Traditional origins: Played for generations in Italy
1870: American variation described by Cavendish in Westminster Chess Papers
1900: Newspaper article describes American version played by Italian immigrants
Modern Era: Still played in Italy; rules widely documented in English and Italian.
history.cultural: Part of the rich Italian trick-taking game tradition. The unusual card ranking (3 high) is characteristic of several Italian games. Related to Tressette, Mediatore, and Spizzichino.
history.evolution: The game has remained relatively stable in Italy. An American variation with rationalized scoring existed among Italian immigrants in the late 19th century but may no longer be played.

rules.objective: Capture aces (worth 1 point each) and win the last trick (worth 1 point). Total 5 points per hand. First to 11 or 21 points wins the game.
rules.gameplay: The game is a point-trick game with bidding. Players bid to determine who plays alone against the other two. The bidder must capture at least 3 of the 5 available points (the four aces and the last trick). Cards are played in tricks with no trumps. Players must follow suit if possible. Highest card of led suit wins the trick. Winner leads to next trick.
keyRules: 13 cards each, dealer takes 14 and discards 1
Bidding to play alone against other two
No trumps - follow suit, highest card wins
Capture aces (1 point each) and last trick (1 point)

strategy.basic: Try to capture aces by winning tricks when they are played. The last trick is crucial - save a high card for it. When bidding, assess whether you can capture 3 of the 5 points.
strategy.intermediate: Count cards to track which aces have been played. Coordinate with partner when defending against the bidder. When bidding, consider your ace holdings and endgame potential. The 3s and 2s are the most powerful cards.
strategy.advanced: Sophisticated bidding based on hand evaluation. Card counting to track all high cards. Strategic play to force out opponents' high cards. Endgame technique for securing the last trick.
tips: Save a high card (3, 2, or Ace) for the last trick
Track which aces have been played
When defending, cooperate with partner to stop bidder
Don't bid unless you have a good chance at 3+ points
The 3s are the most powerful cards - use them wisely
Try to capture aces early before opponents can protect them

scoring.description: Points available: Each ace captured = 1 point (4 points total). Winning last trick = 1 point. Total 5 points per hand. If bidder makes at least 3 points: scores points captured by all players. If bidder fails (makes 2 or fewer): opponents score their captured points plus 1 bonus point each. Game typically to 11 or 21 points.
